question: The use of AI systems in diagnostic medical devices introduces performance deterioration risks after initial validation. Variations in disease prevalence, acquisition protocols and demographic characteristics can produce dataset shifts, altering sensitivity, specificity and probabilistic calibration, even without causing serious incidents that are immediately identifiable.

Clinical evaluation and post-market surveillance are a requirement under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. In addition, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 regulates high-risk AI systems, according to the applicable conditions and deadlines. What still needs to be clarified is whether cases of deterioration within subgroups of patients, masked by aggregate indicators, can promptly be identified through monitoring.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Which operational metrics and thresholds, including subgroup sensitivity, false negative rate, calibration and confidence intervals are required or planned in order to detect dataset shifts and performance drifts in AI-enabled diagnostic devices?

How is the representativeness of local clinical data checked and what is the distribution of responsibilities between manufacturers and healthcare facilities for ongoing monitoring, even in the absence of reported incidents?
Will it define harmonised criteria for revalidation, recalibration, controlled updating and suspension of use, when performance falls below clinically acceptable thresholds?
